draft.title: Pricing strategies
card: Price skimming
A new product is launched at a high price to earn strong returns from buyers who want it early. The price is lowered later to reach more customers.
Penetration pricing
A new product is launched at a low price to win market share fast. The price may be raised once the business has a loyal customer base.
Loss leader
A product sold at or below cost to bring customers into the shop. The business hopes they will also buy other items at full price.
Price points and bundling
Price points set prices just under a round figure, such as $9.95, so they look lower. Price bundling sells several items together for one price, which is often lower than buying each one separately.
draft.remember: Skimming starts high, penetration starts low, and loss leaders and bundles draw customers in.

a.q: Zane launches a new gaming headset at a low price so it quickly wins a large share of the market. Which strategy is this?
opts: Penetration pricing
Price skimming
Loss leader pricing
Price bundling
a.why: A low launch price used to win market share is penetration pricing. Skimming is the opposite, because it starts high to earn strong returns from early buyers.
a.clue: Think about whether the launch price is high or low, and why.

b.q: A supermarket in Orange sells milk at below cost, hoping shoppers will also fill their trolleys with other goods. Which strategy is this, and why is it used?
opts: Loss leader, to bring customers into the store
Penetration, to win market share for the milk
Skimming, to earn strong returns from early buyers
Price bundling, to sell several items for one price
b.why: Selling milk below cost to attract shoppers who then buy other items is a loss leader. Penetration pricing is tempting, but it is used for a new product to win share, not to draw customers in to buy other items.
b.clue: The business expects to make its money on other items, not on the milk.

b.best: Loss leader, to bring customers into the store

problems.detail: In NSW HSC Business Studies resources, 'price points' usually means setting a few set price levels across a product range (for example $50, $80 and $120). The card instead describes charm or psychological pricing ($9.95 just under a round figure). This may teach students the wrong meaning of a syllabus term.
